(p-158)

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Surat al-Falaq (The Daybreak)

It has been said: when Allah, exalted is He, declared pure monotheism in Surat al-Ikhlas (Sincerity), which is the battlefield of faith and polytheism and the source of dispute and enmity between the Prophet (ﷺ) and his enemies, he (ﷺ) was commanded to seek refuge from the evils of creation so that they would not harm him. Etc.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of the daybreak.﴾

Abu Hayyan and others said: al-falaq (الفَلَقُ) is of the pattern fa'al with the meaning of maf'ul (مَفْعُول), i.e., maflub (مَفْلُوق), "split." Scholars differed about what is meant by it.

It was said: it is the dawn, from which the night is split.

It was said: it is the grain and the date-stone.

It was said: it is a pit in Hell.

Some exegetes said: it is everything that Allah has split from something else, such as the night from the dawn, the grain and the date-stone from the plant, the earth from the vegetation, the mountains from the rivers, the wombs from the offspring, and the clouds from the rain.

Ibn Jarir said: Allah stated it without restriction, so it should be taken without restriction as He stated it.

What appears is that all the opinions, except the view that it is a pit in Hell, are of the type of ikhtilaf al-tanawwu' (variation of diversity, meaning different expressions of one meaning), and that they are all possible. Ibn Jarir said this in general terms.

As for the view that it is a pit in Hell, no text has been established for it, and there is no observable phenomenon to which one may refer as evidence of the power of Allah, exalted is He, as there is in the other observable things.

(p-159) What the Qur'an supports is the first view, as the clear text came concerning the dawn and the grain and the date-stone, such as His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah is the splitter of the grain and the date-stone. He brings the living out of the dead and brings the dead out of the living. That is Allah; so how are you deluded?﴾ ﴿He is the splitter of the daybreak, and He made the night for rest and the sun and the moon for reckoning. That is the decree of the Almighty, the All-Knowing.﴾ [al-An'am: 95-96].

All of these are signs indicating the power of Allah. And it came in the hadith of 'Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, concerning the beginning of revelation, that the Prophet (ﷺ) did not see a dream except that it came like the splitting of the dawn (falaq al-subh).

Al-falaq, meaning "the dawn," is well known in the speech of the Arabs.

On this is the saying of the poet:

"O night which I did not sleep through; I spent it awaiting, watching the stars until the daybreak had appeared."

And the saying of another, similar to it, in which it says: "until the daybreak shone forth" instead of "had appeared." In reality, it carries the force of an oath by the Lord of the whole universe, in which some of it splits from other parts.

The Exalted said: ﴿From the evil of what He has created﴾. This is general, and it remains on its general scope, to the extent that al-Hasan said: "Indeed Iblis and Hell are among what He has created."

The Mu'tazilah (a rationalist theological school) have an argument about this verse concerning the creation of the acts of the servants, and that God does not create evil. They said: "How can He create it and decree it, and then command seeking refuge in Him, glorified is He, from what He has created and decreed?"

The People of the Sunnah (Ahl al-Sunnah, the orthodox majority) answered: "There is no obstacle to this, as in the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): 'And I seek refuge in You from You.'"

The Exalted has also said: ﴿God is the Creator of everything﴾ [al-Ra'd: 16].

The Shaykh, may God's mercy be upon us and upon him, had previously discussed this issue in the debate between al-Isfara'ini and al-Jubba'i concerning destiny (qadar).

It is well known that nothing whatsoever comes from a created being except by the will of the Creator, ﴿And you do not will except that God wills﴾.

**The Qur'anic verse:** ﴿And from the evil of darkness when it settles﴾.

(p-160) *Al-Ghasiq* (الغاسِق): it is said that it means the night, based on the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Establish the prayer at the decline of the sun until the darkness of the night﴾ [al-Isra: 78].

*Waqab* (وَقَبَ): i.e., it entered.

On this meaning is the verse of the poet:

*"Indeed this night has grown dark (ghasaqa), and I have complained of worry and sleeplessness."*

And the verse of another:

*"O phantom of Hind, you have left me sleepless, when you came to us as a visitor while the night had grown dark."*

Al-Qurtubi said: This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak, Qatadah, al-Suddi, and others.

It was also said: *al-Ghasiq* is the moon when it is at the end of the month, based on the hadith of 'A'ishah in al-Tirmidhi, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to her: "Seek refuge from this, for it is *al-ghasiq* when it *waqab*." That is, the moon.

The one who holds this view says that it is more fitting to what comes after it, namely sorcery, because it is most prevalent among them at the end of the month.

Al-Qurtubi also related from Tha'lab, from Ibn al-A'rabi, that the people of mischief watch for the *wajbat* of the moon, that is, its setting and its disappearance.

He also cited the verse of the poet:

*"Allah has relieved me of things I dislike: among them the old woman, and among them the dog, and the moon.*

*This one barks, and this one is lit by, and this one is a solid, strong-bodied woman who keeps up the night's vigil."*

*Al-Damraz* (الضَّمْرَز): the aged she-camel, and the coarse, heavy-set woman.

The correct view is the first, which is that it means the night, by the testimony of the Qur'an.

The second view follows from it, because the moon's appearing and disappearing is tied to the night, so it is part of what happens in the night. In the night, the devils and the people of corruption, among both humans and animals, spread out, and there is little to help except Allah.

(p-161) In a hadith: "Extinguish the lamps, for the *fuwaysiqa* (الفُوَيْسِقَة) sets the people's houses on fire at night." That is, the mouse.

The commentary on His words, the Exalted: ﴿And from the evil of those who blow on knots﴾.

What is meant by it is definitely sorcerers, whether the blowing is by women, as the apparent wording suggests, or by men, in the sense of groups, or by evil souls, so that it includes both kinds.

The exegetes agreed that it was revealed concerning Labid ibn al-A'sam, when he bewitched the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Then Jibril, peace be upon him, came to him and informed him.

The Shaykh, may Allah's mercy be upon us and upon him, has already discussed the topic of magic (sihr), its types, its rulings, and everything related to it, when commenting on the words of the Exalted: ﴿And the sorcerer does not succeed, wherever he comes﴾ [Ta-Ha: 69], in Surat Ta-Ha, except for one issue, which is the ruling if someone kills or destroys something by his magic, what its ruling is. We present it briefly.

Issue

Ibn Qudamah mentioned in al-Mughni, may Allah have mercy on him, the sixth type of killing: that he kills someone by magic that usually kills, so retaliation (qawad) becomes obligatory for him. If it is of a kind that does not usually kill, then the blood money (diyah) is due. End of quote.

Al-Nawawi mentioned in al-Minhaj, the commentary on Mughni al-Muhtaj for the Shafi'is, the indication that he is killed in that case as well.

Ibn Hajar mentioned the same in al-Fath: that the sorcerer is killed if he kills by his magic.

Note

The effect of magic falls upon animals just as it falls upon humans.

Abu Hayyan said: Someone who saw, in some of the desert, with some people, a red thread in which knots had been tied on young camels (fusan, the plural of fasil), so they were prevented from suckling their mothers by this. Whenever he untied a knot, that young camel would run to its mother immediately and suckle. End of quote.

Likewise, envy (hasad) also falls upon animals, and even upon inanimate things. That is, the evil eye of the one who casts it affects animals, inanimate objects, and plants, just as it affects humans, as will come later, God willing. (p-١٦٢)

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 113, verse 5 (part 1 of 2):

The Almighty's saying: ﴿And from the evil of an envier when he envies﴾.

The coupling of envy (ḥasad) with sorcery (siḥr) here indicates that there is a connection between each of sorcery and envy. The least that can be said is that both involve a hidden influence: from the sorcerer through sorcery, and from the envier through envy, with the shared characteristic of general harm. Both are the infliction of harm in secret, and both are forbidden.

Our shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him and bestow His favour upon us and upon him, has clarified the types of sorcery and its rulings and has presented a comprehensive discussion of it.

It has become clear from what we have presented that envy has a connection with sorcery to some degree. It is therefore necessary to clarify it and explain its matter as far as possible, God willing.

First: its definition. They said: envy is wishing for the removal of another's blessing, or wishing that the blessing not come to another out of stinginess toward him with it.

Seeking refuge from the evil of the envier "when he envies" is restricted, i.e., at the moment he actually inflicts envy. In contrast, the refuge from the evil of the sorcerer is not restricted by "when he works sorcery."

And Allah knows best: blowing into knots is itself the very essence of sorcery, so seeking refuge is placed in its proper position at the time of his sorcery, which proceeds from him through his blowing that takes effect in the knots.

As for the envier, one seeks refuge from him only when he actually inflicts envy, i.e., when he directs it toward the envied person, because before he directs envy at the envied person no evil can proceed from him, so there is no place for seeking refuge from him.

As for the reality of envy: it is impossible to define it logically.

It has already been mentioned that the shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him and bestow His favour upon us and upon him, said about sorcery that it cannot be defined because of its hiddenness.

It is well known that envy is even more hidden, because it is an inner act and a heart-born effect. It has been said of it that it is like an invisible radiation that passes from the heart of the envier to the envied, when he burns in his heart over the envied person. The envy of the envier has been likened to fire in their saying:

"Bear patiently the sting of the envious, for your patience is its killer.
Like fire it consumes its own self, if it does not find something else to consume."

Some philosophers denied the occurrence of envy, since it is not observed, and they are refuted by every existing thing that is not observed, such as the soul, the spirit, and the intellect.

X-rays have been observed today, though they are not visible, yet they penetrate into the interior of the body of a human being and an animal, and even wood and the like. Only lead stops them, because of the density of its metal. So imagine the interior of a human body with its bones, intestines and other organs. There is no sense in rejecting something merely because it is not seen.

A NOTE

Envy has been mentioned here without specifying what it is directed at, although, as has preceded, it is the removal of a blessing from another.

The Noble Qur'an has drawn attention to the greatest blessings for which the Muslims in general, and the Messenger (ﷺ) in particular, were envied: the blessing of Islam, the blessing of revelation, and the acquisition of spoils.

The People of the Book envied the Muslims for Islam, in the saying of the Most High: ﴿Many of the People of the Book wish they could turn you back to disbelief after you have believed, out of envy from themselves, after the truth has become clear to them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 109].

The polytheists envied the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for the blessing of revelation sent to him, as in the saying of the Most High: ﴿Or do they envy the people for what Allah has given them of His bounty?﴾ [al-Nisa: 54].

"The people" here is a general term used to mean a specific individual, namely the Prophet (ﷺ), as in the saying of the Most High: ﴿Those to whom the people said, "Indeed the people have gathered against you"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 173].

So the first "the people" is a general term used to mean one specific man, who is Nu'aym ibn Mas'ud al-Ashja'i.

Among what envy has been reported regarding is a blessing that is anticipated.

The Most High said: ﴿The ones who stayed behind will say when you set out to take spoils, "Let us follow you." They wish to change the word of Allah. Say, "You will not follow us; Allah has said this before." Then they will say, "Rather, you envy us." Rather, they understand but little﴾ [al-Fath: 15].

Thus the text of the Qur'an makes clear that envy may occur regarding an existing blessing, and it may occur regarding a blessing whose existence is expected.

ANOTHER NOTE

The evil eye exists just as envy exists, and I have not found anyone who distinguished between them, although there is a difference.

It has come in the Sahih: "Indeed the evil eye is real." [Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim]

And it has come in the Sunan: "If anything could outrun the decree, the evil eye would have outrun it." [Sunan al-Tirmidhi]

Regarding envy one says ḥāsid (envier), and regarding the evil eye one says ʿā'in (one who afflicts with the evil eye). They share the effect but differ in the means and the point of origin.

The envier may envy what he has not seen, and he may envy a matter that is anticipated before it occurs. Its source is the burning of the heart and the regarding of a blessing on the envied person as too great, along with wishing for its removal from him or for its not reaching him. This is an extreme degradation of the soul.

The one who afflicts with the evil eye only afflicts what he sees and what exists in fact. Its source is the emission of a glance from the eye. He may afflict what he dislikes to be harmed by, such as his child or his property.

Envy may also be applied to the evil eye, and the word ḥasad may be used to mean ghibṭah (admiring desire), which is wishing for what one sees in others without wishing for its removal from them.

On this basis is the hadith: "There is no envy except in two: a man whom Allah has given wealth and has empowered him to spend it in good, and a man whom Allah has given wisdom and who judges by it among people."

Al-Qurtubi said: It has been narrated with a raised chain: "The believer admires, and the hypocrite envies."

He also said: Envy was the first sin by which Allah was disobeyed in heaven, and the first sin by which He was disobeyed on earth: Iblis envied Adam, and Qabil envied Habil. End of quote.

A WARNING

I heard from our shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him and bestow His favour upon us and upon him, his saying: the first sin committed was envy, and its evil consequences extended to other sins. That was when Iblis envied our father Adam for the honours Allah had given him among His creation, by creating him with His own hands and commanding the angels to prostrate to him. Envy led him to arrogance, and arrogance prevented him from complying with the command to prostrate, so the result was his expulsion. We seek refuge with Allah.

THE CAUSES OF ENVY

By reflecting on the story, it becomes apparent that the underlying impetus for envy is two matters:

The first: belittling the envied person.

The second: the envier's self-admiration, as Iblis said, giving as the reason for his refusal to prostrate: ﴿I am better than him﴾ [al-A'raf: 12].

Then he explained the claimed superiority in his saying: ﴿You created me from fire and created him from clay﴾ [al-A'raf: 12]. All the other causes are included in this.

They have mentioned among these causes: self-glorification, not wanting anyone to rise above him; self-admiration, such that he sees no one as more deserving than himself; fear of losing one's aims when one sees a person who will become independent of him; and love of leadership, in the case of someone who does not want anyone to precede him in any field or domain.

Al-Razi mentioned these, quoting from al-Ghazali.

From here we see that no one who is self-admiring ever fails to belittle others and envy them for even the slightest blessing Allah has bestowed upon them. May Allah protect us from that.

A NOTE

If the first sin committed was the envy of Iblis toward our father Adam for what Allah had bestowed upon him, and if the envy of the polytheists toward the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came regarding the blessing of revelation, and the envy of the People of the Book toward the Muslims came regarding the blessing of Islam, and if this sura came at the end of the Qur'an, then it is as though it came after the Qur'an to remind the Muslims of the magnitude of His blessing upon them and the intensity of the envy directed at it, so that they may beware of their enemies who plot against them in their religion, from both the jinn and mankind, as will be discussed in the following sura, which is the last one, God willing.

[p-166] A QUESTION ON THE RULING REGARDING ONE WHO KILLS, BREAKS, OR DESTROYS SOMETHING BY THE EVIL EYE

What was explained in regard to sorcery has preceded. As for the evil eye, Ibn Hajar said in Fath al-Bari, in the Book of Medicine, the following text: There has been disagreement over whether retaliation (qisas) applies in this case, meaning by the evil eye.

Al-Qurtubi said: If the one with the evil eye destroys something, he is liable for it. If he kills, then retaliation or blood-money (diyah) is due from him if this is repeated from him, to the point that it becomes his habit. In this respect he is like the sorcerer according to those who do not regard killing by him as disbelief. End of quote.

The Shafi'is did not address retaliation in this matter; rather they prohibited it, and they said: it does not usually kill, and it is not considered something that destroys.

Al-Nawawi said in al-Rawdah: There is no blood-money in it nor expiation (kaffarah), because a ruling is only based on something general and regulated, not on what pertains to some people in some circumstances and has no regulation. How could it be, when no act has occurred from him at all? Its extent is merely envy and a wish for the removal of a blessing.

Also, what results from being struck by the evil eye is the occurrence of something disliked to that person, and that disliked thing is not necessarily the loss of life. It may happen to him through something other than that, as an effect of the evil eye. End of quote.

Nothing disturbs this except the ruling to kill the sorcerer, for it has the same meaning, and the difference between them is difficult to establish.

Ibn Battal reported from some scholars: it is appropriate for the ruler to prevent the one with the evil eye, if he is known for it, from mixing with people, and that he should be required to stay in his house. If he is poor, he should be provided with what sustains him, for his harm is greater than the harm of the leper whom ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, ordered to be kept from mixing with people, and greater than the harm of garlic, whose eater the Lawgiver prevented from attending congregational prayer.

Al-Nawawi said: This view is sound and definite; no statement contrary to it is known from anyone else. End of quote from Fath al-Bari.

Upon careful reflection on the statements of al-Qurtubi and al-Nawawi, there is no fundamental disagreement between them, since al-Qurtubi restricts his statement to what is repeated from him to the point that it becomes a habit for him.

Al-Nawawi says that it does not usually kill. On this basis, if it were established that it usually kills and this is repeated from him, [p-167] then it agrees completely with the statement of al-Qurtubi that whoever destroys by his eye, and it is habitual for him, is liable. This is a reasonable position, and Allah knows best.

In the Hanbali work Kashshaf al-Qina', the text reads: al-mi'yan is one who kills by his eye.

Ibn Nasr Allah said in the margins of al-Furu': It is appropriate to equate him with the sorcerer who usually kills by his sorcery. So if his eye is capable of killing and he does it by choice, retaliation is due from him. End of quote.

* *

QUESTION: EXPLANATION OF WHAT THE EVIL EYE IS TREATED WITH

Since envy is the most harmful thing to a human being, and being struck by the evil eye is a reality about which there is no doubt, and it has come in the text: "If anything could outrun the decree, the evil eye would have outrun it."

And the hadith: "Indeed the evil eye is real." The Sunnah has explained in detail how to guard against it before it occurs, and how to treat it once it has occurred.

This is found in what Malik narrated in the Muwatta' and others among the Sahih collections, in the hadith of Sahl ibn Hunayf. Al-Bukhari in his Sahih set a chapter heading: "The Chapter on Ruqyah for the Evil Eye," and mentioned the hadith of ʿAʾishah that she said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) ordered me, or ordered that someone be treated by ruqyah for the evil eye."

Malik also set a chapter in the Muwatta' titled "Ablution from the Evil Eye," and another chapter after it titled "Ruqyah for the Evil Eye," and he cited the hadith of Sahl in full, in which is an explanation of how to guard against it and treat it. Therefore we will suffice with citing it in full because of its comprehensiveness.

He said: From Muhammad ibn Abi Umamah ibn Sahl ibn Hunayf, that he heard his father say: "My father Sahl ibn Hunayf bathed at al-Kharrar, and he took off a robe he was wearing, while ʿAmir ibn Rabi'ah was looking on. He said: Sahl was a man with white, fine skin. He said: ʿAmir ibn Rabi'ah said to him: I have never seen anything like today, not even the skin of a virgin. He said: Sahl immediately fell ill and his illness became severe. He was brought to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and they informed him that Sahl had fallen ill and was not able to come with you, O Messenger of Allah. So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came to him and Sahl informed him of what had happened with ʿAmir. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Why does one of you kill his brother? Why did you not invoke blessing? Indeed the evil eye is real. Perform ablution for him.' So ʿAmir performed ablution for him, and Sahl went out with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), with nothing wrong with him."

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 113, verse 5 (part 2 of 2):

(p-168) He related again, in the same narration: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, 'Do you suspect anyone of having done this?' They said, 'We suspect Amir ibn Rabi'ah.' He said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ summoned Amir and became angry with him, and said, 'Why would one of you kill his brother? Why did you not say the blessing (barraka)? Bathe for him.' So Amir washed his face, his hands, his elbows, his knees, and the tips of his feet, and the inner part of his waist-wrap (izar), in a cup; then the water was poured over him, and Sahl went out with the people, with no harm in him.'"

This narration definitively establishes the occurrence of the evil eye (al-'ayn), and this is a matter agreed upon by the people of the Sunnah and the early generations of the Ummah. It also indicates that whoever blesses, i.e., says "Tabaraka Allah" (blessed is Allah), [protects against it].

In some narrations other than Malik's: "Why did you not say takbir (Allahu akbar)?" That is, he should say "Allahu akbar" three times, for that repels the eye of the one who casts the evil eye.

As has come in the Sunnah, "supplication repels calamity." If it is not averted when it occurs and afflicts, then the remedy for it, as mentioned here, is "perform ablution for him" (tawaddaa' lahu), and the other wording is "bathe for him" (ightasil lahu).

The meaning of washing for him has been detailed: it is washing the face and both hands, meaning the two palms only, and the elbows, knees and feet, and the edge of the inner waist-wrap. This is to be done in a vessel that does not let water fall onto the ground, and this water is poured over the afflicted person from behind, and the vessel is tipped over behind him.

Al-Qadi al-Baji mentioned it in detail in his commentary on the Muwatta', saying: It is narrated from Yahya ibn Yahya, from Ibn Nafi', regarding the meaning of the ablution that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ commanded, that he said:

The one suspected of causing the evil eye washes his face, his hands, his elbows, his knees, his feet, and the inner part of his waist-wrap. He said: He does not wash what is between the hand and the elbow, i.e., he does not wash the forearm from the hand.

It is narrated from al-Zuhri that he said: The washing that we found our scholars describing is: the one who casts the evil eye is brought a cup containing water, and he holds it raised above the ground, then he places his palm in it and rinses his mouth, then spits it back into the cup, then washes his face into the cup in a single pouring; then he puts his left hand in and pours with it over his right palm; then he puts his right hand in and pours with it over the back of his left palm in a single pouring; then he puts his left hand in and pours with it over his right elbow; then he puts his right hand in and pours over his left elbow; then he puts his left hand in and pours with it over his right foot; then he puts his right hand in and pours with it over his left foot; then he puts his left hand in and pours with it over his right knee; then he puts his right hand in and pours with it over his left knee; all of this into the cup; then he puts the inner part of his waist-wrap into the cup, and the cup is not set down (p-169) on the ground, and it is poured over the head of the one afflicted, from behind him, in a single pouring. It was also said: he is made heedless and poured over, i.e., while he is in a state of heedlessness. Then the cup is tipped over onto the ground behind him.

As for the inner part of his waist-wrap: it is the hanging end that descends from his waist-wrap to his skin at that place; he passes the right end over the left only, until he ties it with that hanging end which is on the inside. End of quotation.

Among what this hadith guides to is the Prophet's ﷺ anger at Amir ibn Rabi'ah.

His saying ﷺ, "Why would one of you kill his brother?" clarifies the gravity of this act, and that it may indeed cause death.

Among what should be observed by both parties: whoever is afflicted by the evil eye, let him bless when he sees what pleases him, lest he harm anyone with his eye, and lest his eye outrun him.

Likewise, whoever suspects someone of the evil eye, let him say takbir three times when he fears it. For Allah repels the evil eye by that. And praise be to Allah.

They have also mentioned a remedy for envy of the same kind, i.e., the envious person treats himself with it so that he may find rest from the toil of envy that blazes in his heart, troubling his life and bringing sorrow upon him. It consists, in general terms, of two matters: knowledge, then action.

The meaning of knowledge is that he knows with certainty that the blessing he sees upon the envied person is only a gift from Allah by a prior decree and a binding judgment, and that his envy of it changes nothing of that; and that the harm of envy returns to the envier alone, in his religion, because of his non-acceptance of Allah's decree and His distribution among His servants, for in his envy he is like one who objects to the saying of Allah the Exalted: "It is We who apportion among them their livelihood in the life of this world" [al-Zukhruf: 32]; and in his worldly life, because it produces sickness, sorrows and distress, and the people's aversion and hatred of him; and beyond this and that is the punishment in the Hereafter.

As for action, it is striving against the soul's impulses toward envy, as the indication of it has already been given among the causes. So when he sees one who has a blessing and his eye belittles him, let him try to honor him and serve him.

If his soul tempts him to vanity, let him turn it back to humility and showing his need and poverty.

If his soul prompts him to wish for the removal of the blessing from another, let him redirect that to wishing for its like for himself. And Allah's bounty is great.

(p-170) If envy calls him to harm the envied person, let him strive to do good to him. In this way he is spared the severity of envy, and others are spared his evil.

And as in the report: "The believer covets good (yaghbit), and the hypocrite envies (yahsud)."

We ask Allah for well-being and protection.
